video_title: Why Your Trading Strategy Might Be Wrong for You · Alex Temiz and Bao Nguyen
gist: Live Chat With Traders panel in Orlando with MIC founders Alex Temiz and Bao Nguyen on trading process: exponential setup-graded sizing (C/B/A = 1k/5k/20k shares), pre-planned entry/exit/stop/target, broker-enforced max loss, and small-cap red-flag checklists. They note the post-PDT market has become more irrational, adding to winners is not currently rewarded, and the 'first red day' now requires a break of the prior day's low.

themes.theme: Exponential bet sizing by setup grade

insights.claim: Alex Temiz says that using identical size on every setup produced swings of +$10k/-$20k/+$30k/-$20k/+$50k/-$40k and a break-even week; grading setups fixed the inconsistency.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Uniform sizing across setups of different quality destroys edge; size must scale with probability.
insights.quote: I was up 10,000 one day, down 20,000 the next day. Up 30,000, down 20,000, up 50,000 minus 40,000. And at the end of the week, somehow I was break even

insights.claim: Temiz's exponential sizing framework uses roughly 1,000 shares on a C setup, 5,000 on a B setup and 20,000 on an A setup, a 20x difference between C and A grades.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Grade-based share size should differ by an order of magnitude, not by small increments.
insights.quote: on a C setup, let's use a,000 shares. On a B setup, you use 5,000 shares. On A setup, you use 20,000 shares.

insights.claim: Temiz argues that on a true, back-tested A setup, dollar risk should be at least 5-10x normal daily risk (e.g., $100 normal to $500-$1,000), not merely doubled to $200.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Traders who only double risk on best setups leave most of the edge on the table.

insights.claim: Bao Nguyen cautions beginners not to jump straight to sizing multiples; size should ramp gradually after back-testing and building trust in a setup, because Alex's A setup may be someone else's worst setup.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Copying a mentor's size without your own data on the setup is a path to large losses.
insights.quote: If you do not know what your best setup is, you have not earned the ability to size up.

insights.claim: Temiz frames setup quality with a 'Bao at Disney World (50%) vs Bao at the club (99%)' analogy: bet heavy only on near-certain setups and light on coin-flips.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Explicit probability estimation per setup is the precondition for variable sizing.

insights.claim: Nguyen compares trading to blackjack where you can see your cards before betting: wait for 18-20 hands, start with a small bet and add only on confirmation, and never go all in because 20 still loses to 21.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Trading's key advantage over casino games is discretionary bet timing and scaling into winners.
insights.quote: Unlike a blackjack, blackjack makes you forced to bet blind, right? You're not betting blind, guys.

insights.claim: Temiz observes that across 250 trading days, maximum aggression is warranted only once or twice a year, yet most traders are aggressive on 248 days and timid on the two that matter.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Most retail P&L damage comes from over-aggression on ordinary days.
insights.quote: There's 250 trading days in the year. 248 of them, you should really probably not be that aggressive.

insights.claim: Temiz says the biggest barrier for most traders is size rather than strategy: if you can't succeed with 50 shares you won't with 1,000-10,000, and cutting size in half would make most traders successful.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Size reduction is the highest-ROI fix for struggling traders.
insights.quote: if you cannot be successful with 50 shares, you will never be successful with a,000 shares, 5,000 shares, 10,000 shares.

insights.claim: Temiz's scaling method: take a 10-15% starter; add only on confirmation signals (for shorts: break under VWAP, a 'death candle', low-of-day break) and exit on invalidation (VWAP reclaim, death-candle reclaim, high-of-day break), with win odds rising roughly 50% to 75% to 90% as signals stack.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Confirmation-based adds let traders be aggressive without front-loading risk.

insights.claim: Temiz, citing coaching from Dr. Brett Steenbarger, says nervousness in a trade means one of four things is unplanned: entry, exit, stop or target; he wrote all four on a post-it note per watch-list stock.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: A written four-point plan per ticker before the open removes in-trade emotional decision making.
insights.quote: that means that you have not planned one of four things. Your entry, your exit, your stop, or your target.

insights.claim: Nguyen trades with pre-placed limit 'fantasy orders' and argues fear comes from the unknown; knowing maximum loss in advance via math eliminates fear, and if scared you should size down.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Pre-committed orders convert discretionary trading into execution of a plan.
insights.quote: I already put out my orders. I call them fantasy orders.

insights.claim: Nguyen says the trade-off is mechanical: smaller size with a wider range produces the same dollar outcome as big size with a tight range, and most traders do better small and capturing more of the move.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Wider stops with smaller size reduce noise stop-outs without raising dollar risk.

insights.claim: Nguyen's rule of thumb: to make 10 cents you need a 20-cent range, and Temiz adds that on a stock with a $1 range a stop should be ~50 cents, not 10 cents.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Target and stop distances must be scaled to the instrument's range to avoid being shaken out.
insights.quote: if you want 10 cents you need a 20 cent range

insights.claim: Nguyen dismisses stop-hunting fears for small accounts but says he avoids round-number stops (e.g., uses $2.14 rather than $2.00) because herd stops cluster there.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Place stops off obvious round levels to avoid clustered liquidity sweeps.
insights.quote: Everybody stops at two bucks. Why the [ __ ] are you doing at two?

insights.claim: Nguyen insists on broker-level max loss and per-ticker auto-liquidation (via Cobra) and says premarket has no auto-liquidation, so premarket trading carries uncapped risk.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Hard broker-enforced loss caps are the only reliable defense against blow-ups.
insights.quote: If you're trading premarket, there's no auto liquidation premarket.

insights.claim: Nguyen recounts a stock (XHG) going from about $1 to $18, and another (ENSC) where NASDAQ busted trades, leaving him unexpectedly long after he thought he had profited; he warns never to rely on trade busts.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Extreme small-cap spikes carry operational risks (trade breaks) beyond price risk.
insights.quote: So the bust never rely on the busting.

insights.claim: Nguyen says stops can be time-based (e.g., cover shorts by 10:30 or before a 3pm spike) and partial, eating small losses along the way rather than all at once.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Stop-loss design includes time and partial exits, not just a single price.

insights.claim: Nguyen advises thinking about the exit first: if the next support line is too close, the trade risks large upside for a tiny win and shouldn't be entered.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Reward-distance check before entry filters out poor risk/reward trades.

insights.claim: Temiz narrows ~17,000 moving stocks to about four on his daily watch list and says members who trade off-list (e.g., going long silver on the day he made $100k shorting gold) consistently lose.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Disciplined universe restriction is itself an edge.

insights.claim: Temiz's red-flag list for small-cap trades: float under 1 million shares, Chinese stocks, ADRs, SSR on, day-one runners, high short float, high institutional ownership, and press releases signalling serial pivots (AI to crypto to marijuana).
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: A checklist of disqualifiers prevents trading structurally dangerous tickers.
insights.quote: number one is low float, less than 1 million share float. Chinese stocks have been very, very risky. ADR stocks have been very, very risky.

insights.claim: Temiz argues shorting a hyped stock on day one is like fighting a young Mike Tyson; day two, when hype fades, offers better odds and sometimes clean 50% fades with no bounces.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: For momentum shorts, waiting for day two trades off some upside for much better odds.
insights.quote: You don't want to be fighting Mike Tyson from 20 years ago, but day two is Mike Tyson that fought Jake Paul.

insights.claim: Temiz and Nguyen say they trade 9:30-10:30 and that members who keep trading 'random' names after 10:30 give back morning gains; the less you trade, the more you often make.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Restricting trading to the highest-volume window improves expectancy.
insights.quote: Oftentimes, the less you trade, the more money you make

insights.claim: Nguyen uses AI prompts to replace manual due diligence on small caps: 'why did this stock go up today?', 'is there dilution?', and 'are there upcoming events?', cutting research that took ages to about 30 seconds.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: LLM-assisted dilution/catalyst checks are becoming a standard retail day-trading edge.
insights.quote: Holy crap, that used to take us forever, dude. Now it's like a 30 seconds.

insights.claim: Nguyen predicts AI will replace back-room due-diligence finance analysts.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Junior research roles in finance face displacement by LLM tooling.
insights.quote: AI is going to replace all of the backroom due diligence finance analyst people

insights.claim: Nguyen says he avoids shorting stocks running ahead of a known event like an investor conference next week, preferring to short on the event day (buy the rumor, sell the news).
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Catalyst calendars matter for timing short entries in small caps.

themes.theme: Market regime changes: post-PDT and evolving setups

insights.claim: Temiz says since the PDT rule went away, small-cap moves have become more irrational and crazier due to many more market participants.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Removal of the pattern-day-trader rule has increased retail-driven volatility in small caps.
insights.quote: ever since PDT went away, a lot of these moves are way more irrational

insights.claim: Temiz says adding to winners currently isn't rewarded because stocks keep reclaiming, so he has shifted to 'nail and bail' singles, whereas six months ago adding to winners massively improved P&L.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Strategy must adapt to regime: in the current cycle, take profits quickly.
insights.quote: right now, adding to a winner is not rewarding.

insights.claim: Temiz says the 'first red day' setup has evolved: it now requires the stock to both go red and break below the previous day's low, as seen on CAR (Avis) this year.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Classic setups decay; adding a prior-day-low break filter restores the first-red-day edge.
insights.quote: The new trick is not only does it have to go red, it has to go under the previous day's lows.

insights.claim: Nguyen says small caps are no longer all-day faders and can reclaim to much higher levels, so he scalps ~20 cents on dollar stocks (20%) rather than holding for the backside, and the 'low-hanging fruit' day-two continuation short has periodically stopped working.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Backside-holding short strategies in sub-$5 names carry more squeeze risk now.

insights.claim: Temiz cites silver, gold, oil and CAR as the big trading opportunities of this year.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Macro commodity moves have been a major day-trading opportunity set in 2026.

insights.claim: Temiz argues AI will not eliminate trading edges because inefficiencies always remain; it may reduce edge in one place but increase it elsewhere, and AI is only as good as its training data.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Discretionary traders should use AI as a tool rather than fear displacement.
insights.quote: It may reduce the amount of edge in one place but it'll probably increase the amount of edge somewhere else.

themes.theme: Personal style, account management and psychology

insights.claim: Temiz and Nguyen trade the same stocks at similar levels but very differently: Nguyen runs ~10-20 names with quick partials and adds liquidity, while Temiz focuses on one stock with full attention and removes liquidity on winners.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Strategy execution should match personality and attention capacity.
insights.quote: If BA was trading 10 stocks, he has 10% attention on every single stock.

insights.claim: Nguyen prefers to make $10,000/day via ~15 trades of $500 each rather than one $10,000 trade, and suggests traders scale by finding more setups that earn their reliable amount before sizing up.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Scaling breadth of a proven small edge can be safer than scaling depth.

insights.claim: Temiz builds a realized P&L cushion by taking partials early and says his biggest trades come after locking in some profit, which gives him confidence to risk those profits.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Early partials fund later aggression psychologically and financially.
insights.quote: my biggest trades come after I lock in a little bit of profit

insights.claim: Temiz wires out profits regularly (previously keeping a ~$35k account and wiring $15k each time it reached $50k; now about half of weekly gains), arguing you are rich with money in your bank account, not your trading account.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Regular withdrawals cap blow-up exposure as the account grows.
insights.quote: You are rich with the money in your bank account.

insights.claim: Temiz says $1,000/day equals ~$250k a year and $4,000/day ~ $1M a year; his comfort zone is $1k-$10k daily and he declines $20-50k/day because stress rises directly with size.
insights.speaker: Alex Temiz
insights.so_what: Optimal size is bounded by stress tolerance, not just capital.
insights.quote: $1,000 a day is $250k a year. $4,000 a day is a million dollar a year.

insights.claim: Nguyen says the most dangerous trades come after a hot green streak, and that making money while breaking rules (adding to losers, doubling down) predicts long-term failure.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Review whether profits came from rule-following, not just whether a day was green.
insights.quote: the most dangerous trade is the ones where you've been on a hot green streak

insights.claim: Nguyen says his biggest day started down $10,000 and ended up $1.5 million, and that he once had a year with only seven losses.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Outsized days come from process, per the speaker, not from targeting them.
insights.quote: my biggest day I started down $10,000. Then at the end of that day, 1.5 million.

insights.claim: Nguyen advises not quitting a day job until supplemental trading income exceeds it, and says the road to $1,000/day is first making $50/day consistently.
insights.speaker: Bao Nguyen
insights.so_what: Gradual income ramp reduces pressure-driven overtrading.
